title: Trigonometric Functions
lead: Radians measure an angle by the arc it cuts off on the unit circle. From a point on that circle, and from the sides of a right triangle, the six trigonometric functions are defined; their main identities are listed and used to solve equations; and their graphs are read for period, amplitude and shift.
objectives: Convert angle measures between degrees and radians.
Recognize the triangular and circular definitions of the basic trigonometric functions.
Identify the graphs and periods of the trigonometric functions.
Describe the shift of a sine or cosine graph from the equation of the function.
summary_html:
• Radian measure is defined such that the angle associated with the arc of length 1 on the unit circle has radian measure 1. An angle with a degree measure of $180^{\circ}$ has a radian measure of $\pi$ rad.
  • For acute angles $\ktheta,$ the values of the trigonometric functions are defined as ratios of two sides of a right triangle in which one of the acute angles is $\ktheta.$
  • For a general angle $\ktheta,$ let $(x,y)$ be a point on a circle of radius $r$ corresponding to this angle $\ktheta.$ The trigonometric functions can be written as ratios involving $x,y,$ and $r.$
  • The trigonometric functions are periodic. The sine, cosine, secant, and cosecant functions have period $2\pi.$ The tangent and cotangent functions have period $\pi.$

(Figure 1.31) The angle θ is in standard position. The values of the trigonometric functions for θ are defined in terms of the coordinates x and y. (Figure 1.32) For a point P=(x,y) on a circle of radius r, the coordinates x and y satisfy x=r cos θ and y=r sin θ.
By inscribing a right triangle in a circle, we can express the ratios of the side lengths in terms of the trigonometric functions evaluated at θ.

exercises.prompt: Find all solutions to the equation $\cos(2\theta)=\sin\theta.$

answer.solution: Use the double-angle formula for cosine. $\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}+2n\pi,\ \frac{\pi}{6}+2n\pi,\ \frac{5\pi}{6}+2n\pi$ for $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,\ldots$

exercises.prompt: Prove the trigonometric identity $1+\cot^{2}\theta=\csc^{2}\theta.$

answer.solution: Divide both sides of the identity $\sin^{2}\theta+\cos^{2}\theta=1$ by $\sin^{2}\theta.$ $\begin{array}{lll}1+\theta & = & 1+\frac{\theta}{\theta}\\ & = & \frac{\theta}{\theta}+\frac{\theta}{\theta}\\ & = & \frac{\theta+\theta}{\theta}\\ & = & \frac{1}{\theta}\\ & = & \theta\end{array}$<sup class="fn" data-note="c-cp21"></sup>

exercises.prompt: Describe the relationship between the graph of $f(x)=3\sin(4x)-5$ and the graph of $y=\sin(x).$

answer.solution: The graph of $f$ can be sketched using the graph of $y=\sin(x)$ and a sequence of three transformations. To graph $f(x)=3\sin(4x)-5,$ the graph of $y=\sin(x)$ needs to be compressed horizontally by a factor of 4, then stretched vertically by a factor of 3, then shifted down 5 units. The function $f$ will have a period of $\pi/2$ and an amplitude of 3.

For the following exercises, verify that each equation is an identity.

$\frac{\tan\theta\cot\theta}{\csc\theta}=\sin\theta$

answer.solution: By the ratio identities, $\tan\theta\cot\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\cdot\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}=1,$ so the left-hand side is $\frac{1}{\csc\theta}.$ By the reciprocal identity $\csc\theta=\frac{1}{\sin\theta},$ $\frac{1}{\csc\theta}=\sin\theta,$ the right-hand side. The identity holds for every $\theta$ at which $\tan\theta,$ $\cot\theta$ and $\csc\theta$ are defined.

exercises.prompt:
For the following exercises, verify that each equation is an identity.

$\frac{\sec^{2}\theta}{\tan\theta}=\sec\theta\csc\theta$

answer.solution: Write both sides in sines and cosines. The left-hand side is $\frac{\sec^{2}\theta}{\tan\theta}=\frac{1}{\cos^{2}\theta}\cdot\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}=\frac{1}{\cos\theta\sin\theta}.$ The right-hand side is $\sec\theta\csc\theta=\frac{1}{\cos\theta}\cdot\frac{1}{\sin\theta}=\frac{1}{\cos\theta\sin\theta}.$ The two sides are equal wherever both are defined.

exercises.prompt:
For the following exercises, verify that each equation is an identity.

$\frac{\sin t}{\csc t}+\frac{\cos t}{\sec t}=1$

answer.solution: Since $\csc t=\frac{1}{\sin t}$ and $\sec t=\frac{1}{\cos t},$ $\frac{\sin t}{\csc t}=\sin^{2}t$ and $\frac{\cos t}{\sec t}=\cos^{2}t.$ The left-hand side is therefore $\sin^{2}t+\cos^{2}t,$ which equals $1$ by the Pythagorean identity.

exercises.prompt:
For the following exercises, verify that each equation is an identity.

$\frac{\sin x}{\cos x+1}+\frac{\cos x-1}{\sin x}=0$

answer.solution: Put the two fractions over the common denominator $\sin x(\cos x+1)$: $\frac{\sin x}{\cos x+1}+\frac{\cos x-1}{\sin x}=\frac{\sin^{2}x+(\cos x-1)(\cos x+1)}{\sin x(\cos x+1)}=\frac{\sin^{2}x+\cos^{2}x-1}{\sin x(\cos x+1)}.$ By the Pythagorean identity $\sin^{2}x+\cos^{2}x=1,$ the numerator is $0,$ so the left-hand side is $0$ wherever it is defined.

exercises.prompt:
For the following exercises, verify that each equation is an identity.

$\cot\gamma+\tan\gamma=\sec\gamma\csc\gamma$

answer.solution: By the ratio identities, $\cot\gamma+\tan\gamma=\frac{\cos\gamma}{\sin\gamma}+\frac{\sin\gamma}{\cos\gamma}=\frac{\cos^{2}\gamma+\sin^{2}\gamma}{\sin\gamma\cos\gamma}=\frac{1}{\sin\gamma\cos\gamma},$ since $\sin^{2}\gamma+\cos^{2}\gamma=1.$ By the reciprocal identities this is $\frac{1}{\cos\gamma}\cdot\frac{1}{\sin\gamma}=\sec\gamma\csc\gamma.$

exercises.prompt:
For the following exercises, verify that each equation is an identity.

$\sin^{2}\beta+\tan^{2}\beta+\cos^{2}\beta=\sec^{2}\beta$

answer.solution: Group the first and third terms: $\sin^{2}\beta+\cos^{2}\beta=1,$ so the left-hand side is $1+\tan^{2}\beta,$ which equals $\sec^{2}\beta$ by the Pythagorean identity $1+\tan^{2}\theta=\sec^{2}\theta.$

exercises.prompt:
For the following exercises, verify that each equation is an identity.

$\frac{1}{1-\sin\alpha}+\frac{1}{1+\sin\alpha}=2\sec^{2}\alpha$

answer.solution: Over the common denominator $(1-\sin\alpha)(1+\sin\alpha)=1-\sin^{2}\alpha,$ the left-hand side is $\frac{(1+\sin\alpha)+(1-\sin\alpha)}{1-\sin^{2}\alpha}=\frac{2}{1-\sin^{2}\alpha}.$ By the Pythagorean identity, $1-\sin^{2}\alpha=\cos^{2}\alpha,$ so this is $\frac{2}{\cos^{2}\alpha}=2\sec^{2}\alpha.$

exercises.prompt:
For the following exercises, verify that each equation is an identity.

$\frac{\tan\theta-\cot\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}=\sec^{2}\theta-\csc^{2}\theta$

answer.solution: Write the numerator in sines and cosines: $\tan\theta-\cot\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}-\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}=\frac{\sin^{2}\theta-\cos^{2}\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}.$ Dividing by $\sin\theta\cos\theta$ gives $\frac{\sin^{2}\theta-\cos^{2}\theta}{\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta}=\frac{\sin^{2}\theta}{\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta}-\frac{\cos^{2}\theta}{\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta}=\frac{1}{\cos^{2}\theta}-\frac{1}{\sin^{2}\theta}=\sec^{2}\theta-\csc^{2}\theta.$

[T] As a point P moves around a circle, the measure of the angle changes. The measure of how fast the angle is changing is called angular speed, $\omega,$ and is given by $\omega=\theta/t,$ where $\theta$ is in radians and t is time. Find the angular speed for the given data. Round to the nearest thousandth. a. $\theta=\frac{7\pi}{4}\;\text{rad},\ t=10$ sec b. $\theta=\frac{3\pi}{5}\;\text{rad},\ t=8$ sec c. $\theta=\frac{2\pi}{9}\;\text{rad},\ t=1$ min d. $\theta=23.76\;\text{rad},\ t=14$ min

answer.solution: a. 0.550 rad/sec b. 0.236 rad/sec c. 0.698 rad/min d. 1.697 rad/min

For the following problems, consider the population of Ocean City, New Jersey, which is cyclical by season.

The population can be modeled by $P(t)=82.5-67.5\cos[(\pi/6)t],$ where $t$ is time in months $(t=0$ represents January 1) and $P$ is population (in thousands). During a year, in what intervals is the population less than 20,000? During what intervals is the population more than 140,000?

answer.solution: The population is less than 20,000 from December 8 through January 23 and more than 140,000 from May 29 through August 2

footnotes.html: The book’s answer prints $\theta$ in place of every function in the chain. It reads $1+\cot^{2}\theta=1+\frac{\cos^{2}\theta}{\sin^{2}\theta}=\frac{\sin^{2}\theta}{\sin^{2}\theta}+\frac{\cos^{2}\theta}{\sin^{2}\theta}=\frac{\sin^{2}\theta+\cos^{2}\theta}{\sin^{2}\theta}=\frac{1}{\sin^{2}\theta}=\csc^{2}\theta.$
